newsitem.title: JAPAN: North Korea's Hwang a soft-spoken intellectual.
newsitem.headline: North Korea's Hwang a soft-spoken intellectual.

text.p: The senior North Korean official who stunned the world by announcing his intention to defect from his Stalinist homeland is known as a soft-spoken and frank intellectual.
But old acquaintances also remember 73-year-old Hwang Jang-yop as "upside down melon."
Touted as the highest-ranking North Korean official ever to defect, Hwang was 24th in North Korea's ruling hierarchy.
Known as an architect of North Korea's state ideology of "Juche," or self-reliance, Hwang is a graduate of Moscow University where he majored in philosophy.

One of 11 members on the powerful Secretariat of the Workers' Party of Korea, Hwang is believed to be a relative of the late Kim Il-sung and was a mentor to his son Kim Jong-il, who now is the defacto leader of the communist state.
Hwang's influence among North Korea's elite also comes from having been a former president of Kim Il Sung University, where Kim Jong-il and all other senior North Korean officials graduated.
Hwang has also been a member of the party's Central Committee since 1970 and was elected chairman of the Supreme People's Assembly three times.

He has been chairman of the Foreign Relations Committee of the Supreme People's Assembly since 1993, visiting China, India, Vietnam, Cuba and various European nations and holding talks with visiting politicians from Japan and the United States.
But while journalists and scholars who have met him describe the communist revolutionary as a quiet and sophisticated scholar, old associates remember Hwang as "upside down melon."
"His nickname used to be 'upside down melon'," South Korea's Chosun Ilbo newspaper quoted Choi Jae-kyung as saying.
Choi was a former student of Hwang at a leading Pyongyang high school and now is a dentist in Seoul.
"We called him that because his head looks like a melon and he would eat the fruit from the bitter stem," Choi said.

"He used to refuse dressing formally and kept his beard," Choi added. "He was a 'coal-miner-style philosopher' with an angry expression on his face, and would give his lectures in an inaudible voice."
Cho Kun-ok, director of Kyungnam University, told Chosun Ilbo he was not too surprised over Hwang's attempted defection.

"In 1948, we staged an anti-government demonstration in Pyongyang and got ourselves into trouble. We went to Hwang and told him we would flee to the South. He said 'Go, and if you like it stay, if not, you can return,'" said Cho.
Before 1953 it was still possible to freely cross the border into the south.
North Korea invaded the South in 1950, supported by China. The South was aided by a U.S.-led United Nations force. The war ended in 1953 with an armistice agreement.
"Almost 50 years later he is now coming south himself," said Cho.
